text: 5-10 is based on Shapley feature explanations (SHAP), which is a model-agnostic method derived from cooperative game theory to explain the contribution of each feature to a model's predictions. It calculates the average marginal contribution of a feature across all possible combinations of features, ensuring a fair distribution of importance. The average marginal contribution in this context refers to the mean increase or decrease in a model's prediction when a specific feature is added to a subset of other features. Figure 5-10. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) Values Demonstrating F Effect on ESS Prediction. Therefore, the developed tool shall answer two questions for the operators. The first question is “under the existing conditions, are the existing WNS and SPB flowrates contributing to the observed ESS”, while the second question is “under the existing conditions, how will ESS change if WNS and SPB flowrates change”. The suggested deployment tool will rely on the pre-trained model. This model can be re-trained on a monthly or bi-weekly basis according to the data collection. To answer the first question, Integration of Data Driven Process Control for Maximizing Energy and Resource Efficiency in WRRFs 45 Shapley values can be used to identify the current contribution of each feature, as shown in Figure 5-11. For Day 2 in the figure as an example, the model prediction for ESS was 34.46 mg TSS/L, the shift of this value from the base value (24.06 mg TSS/L, which is the average) was predicted to be most significantly influenced by the WNS flow rate (W_WNS_Q), followed by SPB flow rate and temperature. In contrast, in Day 1, WNS TSS mainly contributed to increasing ESS to 28.06 mg TSS/L, while WNS and SPB flow rates contributed to lowering it back to 26.25 mg TSS/L. The challenge is that this works only for fitted or trained data. Hence, this can be implemented either by re-training the model on current conditions, or by finding the most similar point in the training dataset using k-nearest neighbor. Day 1 Day 2 Figure 5-11. Contribution of Each Feature to ESS Prediction of Two Different Days. In addition, the model can be fed the current conditions (the input features) as a new instance in addition to all possible flow rates for WNS and SPB, and the algorithm will generate different predictions according the WNS and SPB values. These values can be plotted in a heat map similar to the one in Figure 5-12. The center of the heatmap can be adjusted based on the current ESS. This heat map will answer both questions; if all values are similar to the existing ESS, this means WNS and SPB return flows are not the main contributors to ESS. For the second question, the heat map will identify the zones of operation where low ESS is expected under the existing conditions. 46 The Water Research Foundation Figure 5-12.
